items.title: Testimonial videos that don't sound like testimonials
items.excerpt: How to make a customer testimonial video people believe: let the customer tell their own story, film once the result is real, and ask about them, not you.
items.coverAlt: A finished kitchen at golden hour with a baby's bottle and a set of builder's keys side by side on the new worktop, the garden doors open behind them
items.body:
A testimonial video stops sounding like a testimonial when the customer tells the story of what happened to them, in their own words, instead of praising the business. You film them once the result is real, ask about their situation rather than about you, and cut it as their account. The praise is then implied by the story, and the viewer believes it because they've worked it out for themselves.

Most testimonial videos are a customer on a sofa saying they were really professional and they'd definitely recommend them. It's sincere, and it doesn't land, because every business has one and they all sound the same.

Why do most testimonial videos sound the same?

Because the questions are about the business. Ask someone what it was like working with you and you get adjectives. Professional, friendly, on time, tidy. Lovely to hear and almost impossible to believe, because the viewer knows the business picked its happiest customer and pointed a camera at them.

There's a scripting problem too. When a customer's been handed lines, or asked to say that again but mention the price this time, it shows. People can hear the difference between someone remembering and someone performing.

And trust in second hand praise is wearing thin. BrightLocal's annual consumer survey tracks how many people trust online reviews as much as a personal recommendation, and that figure has dropped a long way in five years. Generic praise gets discounted in any format. Specific stories still get through.

What makes a customer story believable?

Specifics, stakes and a bit of friction. What the person needed, what was at risk, what was hard, and what they've got now. A story with a worry in it is more convincing than one that's all praise, because real projects have worries.

The Nimrod Road film works because of its stakes. A Victorian house in Tooting that had sat empty after the previous owners died. A couple who wanted the period features kept and the ground floor opened up. A project that started in September, with a baby due at the end of November. The work was finished in eight weeks, two weeks inside the estimate. Both homeowners tell it as their account, and anyone weighing up the same decision hears it from people in their own position.

The praise is implied by the story, and the viewer believes it because they've worked it out for themselves.

Who should tell the story, the customer or the business?

The customer, almost always. A business talking about its own quality is the one voice a prospective customer discounts straight away, because it's the voice being paid.

That was the thinking behind Barry Road, a full house renovation in East Dulwich. Every contractor says the same things about themselves: quality, on time, on budget. So the film is the homeowner giving their own account of the job, what they wanted, what it was like to live through, and what they ended up with. We handed the film to them and let them say whatever they were going to say.

The business can still appear, briefly and doing the work. Just don't let it narrate its own reputation.

Which customer should you film?

Not automatically the happiest one. Pick the customer whose situation looks most like the people you want more of. If your best jobs are period houses with tight deadlines, film the family with the period house and the tight deadline. Someone weighing you up should watch it and recognise their own situation.

Look for someone who had something at stake and can talk about it naturally. A worry, a deadline, a previous bad experience with someone else. They don't need to be polished, and the ones who are a bit unsure on camera often come across as the most honest. Most of all, they need to want to do it. A customer doing you a reluctant favour sounds exactly like one.

When should you film a testimonial?

Once the result is real, and ideally while it's still fresh. Both of those renovation films were made after the family had moved back in, so the customer is talking about a home they live in rather than a promise.

The downside of waiting is that the before has gone. At Nimrod Road the before only exists in the original listing photos, so those were cut against the finished rooms. At Barry Road, before and after floorplans were cut in so the scale of the work reads on screen. If there's any chance you'll want a customer film, photograph the start of the job properly. It costs almost nothing, and you can't get it back later.

The best time to plan a testimonial is before the customer has anything to testify about. Annoying, but true.

What should you ask in a testimonial interview?

Ask about them, not you. Questions that tend to open people up:

  • What was going on before you got in touch?
  • What were you most worried about?
  • What was it like day to day while the work was happening?
  • Was there a moment you weren't sure it would work out?
  • What's different now?
  • What would you tell someone in the position you were in?

Then listen, and follow whatever's interesting rather than ticking through the list. Never feed them the answer. If a customer says something in a way that's a bit clunky but true, keep it. The odd stumble is part of why it sounds real. There's more on this in how to make a brand video people actually watch.

How do you get the most from a customer story film?

Use it in the sales conversation, which is where it earns its money. Both renovation films were made as edits a contractor can send to someone deciding whether to trust them with a house. That's a precise job, and it decided how they were cut.

Beyond that, put the full film on the relevant service page, cut a short version for the top of the site, and pull vertical clips for social, where one honest line can carry a post. Ask the customer's permission for every use up front, paid ads included, so you're not chasing them six months later.

If you've got customers whose stories would sell your work better than you can, see the films we've made or tell us about them.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Should customers be paid to appear in a testimonial video?
faqs.a: Generally no, and it's worth avoiding anything that looks like payment for praise. A small thank you for their time is fine, but the value of a testimonial comes from it being freely given. If a customer is paid or given something significant, viewers would reasonably want to know, so be open about it. Choosing customers who genuinely had a good experience makes the question mostly irrelevant.

faqs.q: How long should a customer testimonial video be?
faqs.a: Long enough to tell one story properly, which is usually two to five minutes for the main film. That's what you send in a sales conversation or put on a service page. From the same interview you can cut a sixty to ninety second version for the top of your site and short vertical clips for social, where a single honest line from the customer can work on its own.

faqs.q: What if a customer gets nervous on camera?
faqs.a: Most people do at first, and it usually passes within ten minutes. Run it as a conversation, with no lines to learn and no autocue, and start with easy questions about their situation before anything that matters. Film them somewhere familiar, ideally the place the work was done. If they stumble, carry on rather than restarting, because those natural moments are often what makes it believable.

faqs.q: Do we need a customer's written permission to use their video?
faqs.a: Yes. Get written consent that covers where the film will appear and for how long, including your website, social media and any paid advertising. It protects you and it's fair to them. Agree up front what happens if they later want it taken down, and keep their personal details, like a full address, out of the film unless they're happy for them to be shown.

items.title: Why real people on camera matter more now
items.excerpt: As AI content floods feeds, real people on camera become proof. What the 2026 trust research says, and why documentary films built on real voices land.
items.coverAlt: A well-used shop counter seen from the customer's side, with a hand-written price card, a worn wooden chopping board and an apron hung on a hook, and nobody in frame, as if the owner just stepped out back
items.body:
Real people on camera matter more as AI content floods feeds because they're proof. A generated face can say anything, so it carries no weight. A real founder, a real member of staff or a real customer, filmed where the work actually happens, is evidence that the business exists and stands behind what it says. Research from The Harris Poll UK, published in April 2026, found seven in ten consumers trust adverts made entirely by humans, and that drops to two in ten when an advert is generated by AI alone.

I've believed this for a long time, but the gap is getting wider. The cheaper it gets to make something that looks real, the more a viewer's first question becomes whether it is.

Why do people trust a brand more when they see real people?

Because a person on camera is putting their face to it. They can be recognised, called, held to what they said. That's a risk a business takes on deliberately, and viewers read it as confidence. A stock presenter or a generated spokesperson costs the business nothing to put in front of you, so it proves nothing.

It's also about who's speaking. People have always believed customers and staff more than the company talking about itself. We wrote about why in brand documentary vs corporate video, and it's the same instinct here. Someone in your position, describing what happened to them, is the version people believe.

What happens to trust when AI is involved?

It falls, and it falls further the more of the work AI does. The Harris Poll UK found trust in an advert drops from seven in ten when it's made entirely by humans, to four in ten when AI tools are used, to two in ten when it's generated by AI alone. Six in ten said a person should always be involved in making advertising that uses AI.

The same research picked out what makes people suspicious. Images that look too perfect, scenes that feel unrealistic and small inconsistencies were the most common giveaways. That's an interesting turn. For years, polish was how a brand showed it had spent money. Now flawless can read as fake.

The cheaper it gets to make something that looks real, the more people want to know whether it is.

Does it have to be the founder on camera?

No, and often it's better when it isn't only the founder. The most convincing person in a film is usually the one with the least reason to flatter the business.

On Barry Road it's the homeowner describing a full renovation in their own words, once the family had moved back in. On the Car Planet film for Plug In Stations, the whole thing is the customer talking. The installer never makes the claim about themselves, which is exactly what makes it usable in a sales conversation.

And La Fromagerie carries four people's accounts of the same business. The founder tells how it started, with a wheel of Beaufort in a garden shed, and the cheesemongers and the wholesale side fill in what it is now. Four voices that don't sound rehearsed are harder to doubt than one polished one.

What if you or your team hate being on camera?

Most people do, at first. The good news is that documentary filming doesn't ask anyone to perform. Nothing's read off an autocue, and nobody's asked to do it again with more energy. The interviews are conversations, and the people who are most nervous at the start often give the best answers an hour in, once they've stopped noticing the camera.

Nobody has ever been more relaxed because someone said “just act natural”. A decent conversation does the job far better.

We've written a practical guide to preparing to be filmed for a brand film, and the short version is that you don't need to be good on camera. You need to know your subject, which you already do.

How do documentary films use real people differently?

They let the story come from the people instead of handing them a script. We spend time with a business before filming, work out what the story actually is, and then go and film conversations in the places the business really lives. La Fromagerie was filmed during trading hours, around customers, in cheese rooms that are cold and dark. That's harder work. It also looks exactly like the shop you'd walk into, and no prompt can give you that.

The other difference is time. A documentary leaves room for the pause before someone answers and the work happening at the speed it really happens. Those are the moments that make a viewer feel they're seeing something true, and they're the hardest thing to fake.

Isn't AI content just cheaper to make?

Per piece, yes, and that's exactly the problem with it. When anyone can produce a polished video in an afternoon, polish stops telling the viewer anything about you. Feeds fill up with it, and it all starts to look the same. What can't be produced in an afternoon is access: the people in your business, the place they work and the things they've been through.

A smaller business usually has more of that than it thinks. The owner answers the phone. The person on camera is the person who'll turn up. That's something a big brand with a generated spokesperson can't buy, and it's worth putting on screen while it still stands out.

Is polished production a bad thing now?

No. Craft still matters. A badly lit, badly recorded film of real people tells the viewer you didn't care enough to do it properly. The point of a proper grade, proper sound and a patient edit is to show real people clearly. Smooth them into something that looks generated and you've thrown away the reason they were there.

Where I'd draw the line is anything that makes the person look less like themselves. Heavy retouching, a script they'd never say in real life, a set that looks nothing like where they work. Keep the people real and spend the budget on showing them well. If there's someone in your business people should hear from, tell us about them, or see more of the films we've made on our films page.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Do we need professional actors for a brand film?
faqs.a: No, and for a documentary-style film you'd usually avoid them. The people who actually run the business, work in it or buy from it carry far more weight than anyone hired to play them, because viewers can tell. Actors make sense for scripted adverts and dramatised scenes. For a film meant to build trust, real people with real stories are the stronger choice.

faqs.q: Can we use customers in our brand film?
faqs.a: Yes, and they're often the most convincing people in it. Ask customers who had a genuinely good experience and are happy to talk about it, and film once the result is real. Keep it a conversation rather than a script, and get their written consent to appear and to the footage being used. A customer's own account is the version prospective buyers believe.

faqs.q: How many people should appear in a brand film?
faqs.a: As many as the story needs, which is usually fewer than people expect. One strong voice can carry a short film. A longer documentary often works best with two to four, each adding something the others can't, like the founder's history alongside the people doing the work now. Every extra person needs time on screen, so more voices usually means a longer film.

faqs.q: Is AI ever fine to use in a film about real people?
faqs.a: Yes, behind the scenes. Transcribing interviews, cleaning up audio, drafting captions and reframing clips for social don't change what anyone said or did. The line is making a real person appear to say or do something they didn't, or generating scenes presented as real. That undermines the whole point of filming real people, and platforms like YouTube ask you to label it.

stat.title: How many consumers trust an advert, by who made it
stat.takeaway: Trust drops sharply as AI takes over the work, so a film that shows real people doing real things has more to offer than ever.

items.title: What we keep hearing from businesses about video
items.excerpt: No faces on the website, stock passed off as content, a decision maker who isn't in the room, missed timing and camera nerves. What we hear, and how to fix it.
items.coverAlt: An office team photo frame on a reception desk still holding the stock photo of smiling models that came with it, beside a real, slightly dusty hard hat
items.body:
When businesses talk to us about video, the same handful of things come up again and again, whatever the sector. The work's excellent but there isn't one real face on the website. The content they've got turns out to be stock. The person keen on a film isn't the person who signs it off. The moment that would have made the story has already gone. And nobody wants to be on camera. Every one of these is fixable, usually without spending more.

I'm keeping this general and anonymised. These are patterns, and if you recognise your own business in one, you're in very good company.

Why does great work end up with no faces on the website?

Because the people doing the best work are usually too busy doing it to think about how it looks. You get a site with brilliant project photos, a logo, a phone number and nobody. Or a team page with a row of grey silhouettes.

The trouble is that buyers choose people. For anything expensive or personal, someone wants to know who's turning up, who they'll be dealing with and whether they seem trustworthy. A business with no faces on its site is asking a stranger to trust it blind, and a competitor with a slightly weaker portfolio and a friendly face on the homepage will often win that one.

The fix is smaller than people expect. Proper photos of the team at work, a short film of the founder explaining why they started, and one or two customers talking about the result. That's often a single day. Our Spotlight shoot exists for exactly this.

What's wrong with "we've already got content"?

Often, nothing. But sometimes, when you look properly, the content is stock footage, AI images and a few phone clips from years ago. Stock fills space, but it can't prove anything about you, because the same handshake and the same smiling team in the same glass office appear on hundreds of other sites. People have learned to scroll straight past it.

The test I use is simple. If you swapped your logo for a competitor's, would the content still make sense? If it would, it's doing no work for you. Footage of your actual people, premises and jobs can only belong to you, and that's why people believe it.

The Super Efficient drainage film shows real content made without much fuss. One day on a live job in Enfield, filmed start to finish with no reshoots, became an eight minute YouTube film, a run of vertical shorts and two carousels. Nothing staged, and nothing that could belong to any other company.

Why do video projects stall when someone else decides?

Because the person who gets in touch is often a marketing lead, an office manager or a founder's right hand, and the decision sits with a director, a board or a partner who wasn't on the call. The enthusiasm doesn't travel up the chain. What reaches the decision maker is a line on a spreadsheet with a number next to it.

It's common enough that Wyzowl's annual survey lists being unable to convince key decision makers as one of the reasons marketers give for not using video at all. If that's where you are, give the person deciding something to react to besides a price: the job the film will do, everything that comes out of one shoot, and an example from a similar business. Our free 44-page guide, Before the camera comes out, was written partly for this. Send it upwards.

Better still, get the person who signs it off into a conversation early. Twenty minutes with them saves weeks of relaying questions back and forth.

Somewhere in the UK right now, a brilliant video idea is sitting in the inbox of someone who's on holiday until the 14th.

What happens when the timing window closes?

Lots of stories have a moment, and once it's gone you can't film it again. A building going up. A project finishing. An anniversary. A team that's about to change. A customer in the first weeks after the work's done, while they're still delighted with it.

We see it with renovation films. On Nimrod Road, the family had already moved back in by the time we filmed, so the before only exists in the original listing photos. It still works, because the couple tell it well and the listing photos are cut against the finished rooms. But it shows how easily the most visual part of a story disappears while a business is still deciding.

So when someone says "let's do it next year", I'd ask what will have changed by then. Sometimes nothing, and waiting's fine. Often the scaffolding's down, the event's over or the people involved have moved on. A film takes six to ten weeks from the first conversation, so if there's a date that matters, count backwards from it.

What if nobody wants to be on camera?

Almost nobody does at first. It's the thing we hear most, and it's completely normal. People worry about how they'll look, what they'll say and whether colleagues will take the mickey afterwards.

Almost nobody wants to be on camera at first. It's the thing we hear most, and it's completely normal.

A few things make a real difference. Interviews run as conversations, with nothing to learn. No autocue. Filming people doing the job they're good at, which relaxes them because they're on their own ground. And time. The good material tends to arrive once people stop noticing the camera, which is one reason our films take two to three shoot days rather than an hour.

It doesn't have to be the boss, either. Sometimes the best person in the film is the engineer who explains things clearly, a long serving member of the team, or a customer. If you're the one going on camera and you're dreading it, read how to prepare for being filmed. It's less painful than you're expecting.

Is any of this a reason not to make a film?

Not really. Each of these comes down to planning and permission. The businesses that end up with a film they're proud of tend to decide early what it's for, get the decision maker involved, pick their moment and let real people speak. Budget matters, but less than any of that.

If one of these sounds like your business, tell us where you're stuck. If a film isn't the right spend yet, we'll say so.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Can we make a brand film if the boss won't appear in it?
faqs.a: Yes. The founder or MD doesn't have to be the face of the film, and sometimes someone else tells the story better. An engineer who explains the work clearly, a long serving member of staff or a customer talking about the result can carry a film well. It's worth the boss appearing briefly if they can, because buyers like to know who's in charge, but it isn't essential.

faqs.q: Is stock footage ever fine to use in a business video?
faqs.a: It's fine for small jobs like filling a gap in an explainer or illustrating something you genuinely can't film, such as a general street scene. It shouldn't carry the story. Anything meant to build trust, like who you are, what your work looks like and what customers say, needs real footage of your own people and jobs, because stock can't prove anything about your business specifically.

faqs.q: How do I pitch a video budget to a director or board?
faqs.a: Lead with the job the film will do and the business problem it's tied to, then the price. Show everything that comes from one shoot, such as the main film, short cuts, vertical clips and photography, so the cost reads per use rather than as one video. An example from a similar business helps. Better still, get the decision maker on an early call so questions don't get lost in relay.

faqs.q: What if the best moment for our film has already passed?
faqs.a: You can often still make a strong film. Existing photos, plans and the people who were there can rebuild the before, and a customer talking about a finished result is very convincing. What you lose is the footage of the moment itself. For the future, photograph the start of important projects properly as a habit, even if you're not sure a film will follow.

stat.takeaway: Most of the reasons businesses hold off on video are about doubt, time and planning, which can usually be talked through before anything is spent.

items.title: What AI can and can't do for brand video in 2026
items.excerpt: What AI video tools can genuinely do for a brand in 2026, what they still can't, where they help a production and when you need to tell your audience.
items.coverAlt: A battered cinema camera on a tripod in an empty workshop, with a small robot vacuum parked politely at its feet as if waiting for instructions
items.body:
In 2026, AI is genuinely useful around a video production. It transcribes interviews, helps find the best lines, writes first-draft captions, cleans up audio, reframes footage for different platforms and can generate short, realistic clips with sound. What it can't do is film your actual people, your actual premises and your actual work, and for a brand film that's the whole point. Used for the jobs around the film, it saves time. Used to replace the film, it tends to cost you trust.

I'm not anti AI. I'd be lying if I said the tools weren't impressive, and some of them have made the dull parts of post-production faster. I just think businesses are being sold the wrong half of it.

What can AI video tools actually do now?

Generated video has moved quickly. Google's Veo 3.1 makes eight second clips, with sound generated alongside the picture, at up to 4K. OpenAI, Runway and others have their own models. Give them a decent prompt and you'll get a shot that looks expensive at first glance.

The less glamorous tools are where most of the day-to-day value sits:

  • Transcription. Hours of interview turned into searchable text, so you can find every time someone mentioned a particular customer in seconds.
  • Captions and subtitles. A first draft generated automatically, then checked by a person, because names and technical words still come out wrong.
  • Audio clean-up. Background hum and room noise reduced on interviews recorded in real places.
  • Reframing. A widescreen shot tracked and cropped to vertical for the feed.
  • Small fixes. Extending a shot by a beat, upscaling an old clip, removing something distracting from the corner of a frame.
  • Translation and dubbing. Including dubbing in a cloned version of the speaker's own voice.

Before the shoot, it's a decent thinking partner. Drafting interview questions, pressure-testing a structure, turning a messy brief into a shot list. None of that replaces the research, but it gets you to a first version faster.

What can't AI do for a brand film?

It can't film the thing that happened. A brand film works because it's evidence. That founder really did start in a shed. That customer really did trust you with their house. Those hands really did paint that sign. Generated footage can look like any of those, but it can't be any of them, and the moment a viewer suspects it isn't real, the evidence is gone.

Our Signwriting Jack film is a good test. The whole value is the hand: the brush loading, and a single unbroken line that either works or doesn't. You could generate a lovely shot of a brush making a perfect line. Nobody would care, because the reason to watch is that a person is doing it, live, with no undo button.

An AI signwriter would paint a flawless line every time, and nobody would ever ring it for a quote.

There are practical limits too. Eight second clips have to be stitched together, and keeping a face, a product or a room consistent across many shots is still fiddly. These models don't know your premises, your team or your products. And anything that leans on a real person's face or voice needs their consent, which gets complicated fast.

Do you have to tell people when a video uses AI?

Sometimes, and audiences increasingly expect you to. YouTube's disclosure rules ask creators to label content that makes a real person appear to say or do something they didn't, alters footage of a real event or place, generates a realistic scene that never happened, or uses generated music as the main focus. They don't ask you to disclose using AI for a script, an outline, captions, colour adjustment, upscaling or cloning your own voice for a dub.

In advertising, the UK's existing rules on misleading ads apply whatever tool made the picture. If generated imagery makes a product look better than it is, that's the same problem it always was.

Where does AI genuinely help a production?

In the edit, mostly. An interview-led film gets found in hours of conversation, and anything that makes those hours searchable gives the editor more time to think about the story instead of scrubbing through footage. That's a real gain, and it goes into the film rather than into a shortcut.

It also helps with the cut-downs. Our films come back as a main film, a short cut and six to ten vertical pieces, and reframing and captioning all of those is exactly the kind of repetitive work these tools are good at. A person still checks every frame, but they're checking rather than building from scratch. If you just need to resize a clip yourself, our free video resizer does that in the browser.

Then there are the bits of a film nobody needs to believe are real. A conceptual opening, an abstract background behind a title, a visual metaphor. The Harris Poll UK research quoted above found people are noticeably more comfortable with AI in backgrounds and conceptual elements than in anything meant to look real.

Use AI for the jobs around the film. The moment it replaces the film, it starts costing you trust.

Should a brand use AI generated people or presenters?

For anything where trust is the point, I wouldn't. A generated presenter tells your customer that nobody in the business was willing to stand behind the message. The research backs that instinct up: people trust ads less as AI does more of the work, and they're especially wary in categories where realism is expected, like food, beauty and travel.

There's a reasonable case for it in training material, or quick internal updates that would never have been filmed properly anyway. Just be clear with yourself about the trade.

Will AI make brand films cheaper?

A bit, in places. The edit gets faster in the boring stages, and captions and versioning take less time. But the biggest single cost in a production is still the shoot day, because crew, kit and travel all scale with it, and no tool turns up at your workshop for you. Where it might save you money is in versioning: more cut-downs, subtitled versions in other languages, quicker turnaround on small changes. That's useful. It just isn't where most of the budget goes. We break the rest down in how much a brand film costs. If you want to talk about where AI fits into a film you're planning, honestly or not at all, get in touch.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: Can AI make a full brand film from a script?
faqs.a: It can produce something that looks like one, but not a convincing brand film. Current models generate short clips, around eight seconds for Google's Veo, so a longer piece is stitched from many shots that struggle to stay consistent. More importantly, none of it shows your real people, premises or work, which is what makes a brand film believable. It's better suited to concepts and drafts.

faqs.q: Is it safe to use an AI voiceover on our videos?
faqs.a: It can be, if the voice is properly licensed or it's your own. Cloning your own voice for a dub is something YouTube explicitly says doesn't need disclosing. Cloning anyone else's voice needs their clear permission, and making a real person appear to say something they didn't is exactly the kind of content platforms ask you to label. Check the tool's terms for commercial use too.

faqs.q: Will AI replace video production companies?
faqs.a: It'll replace some kinds of video work, especially generic stock-style footage and simple explainers. It's much less likely to replace filming real people and real places, because that's the part nobody can generate. My honest view is that production companies who use AI for the slow, repetitive jobs and spend the time saved on the story will be in better shape than before.

faqs.q: Do customers notice when a brand uses AI imagery?
faqs.a: Many think they do, and suspicion alone can hurt. In The Harris Poll UK's 2026 research, 46% of consumers said they were confident they could identify AI imagery in advertising, and images that look too perfect or slightly inconsistent were the most common giveaways. Whether or not they're right, an ad that feels generated tends to be trusted less.

items.title: School open day films: what parents look for
items.excerpt: What parents want to see in a school open day or prospectus film, and general UK guidance on consent and safeguarding when you're filming children at school.
items.coverAlt: An empty classroom just after the bell, chairs pushed back at odd angles, a half wiped whiteboard and one forgotten lunchbox on a desk in a shaft of afternoon light
items.body:
Parents want to see what a normal day at your school feels like: how children are treated, how they treat each other, and whether their own child would be happy there. A good school film shows real lessons, real breaktimes and staff and pupils talking in their own words, filmed within your consent and safeguarding policies. A drone shot of the building and a head teacher reading a mission statement won't tell them any of that.

Below is what parents look for, and how to approach consent and safeguarding when you're filming children. The safeguarding part is general guidance based on common UK practice and isn't legal advice. Your school's own policies and your data protection lead come first.

What do parents actually want to see in a school film?

The feeling of the place, more than the facilities list. When the Youth Sport Trust and #BeeWell commissioned YouGov to ask parents what matters when choosing a secondary school, pupil wellbeing came out ahead of Ofsted ratings and exam results. Parents can look up league tables in thirty seconds. What they can't look up is whether children seem happy in the corridors, and that's exactly what film is good at showing.

In practice that means:

  • Ordinary moments. A lesson in full swing, lunch, a club after school, children walking between buildings. The ordinary bits are what a parent pictures their own child doing.
  • How staff talk to children. Tone, patience, a teacher crouching to a child's level. Parents notice it straight away.
  • Pupils speaking for themselves. Older pupils describing what they like and what took getting used to are far more convincing than any line in the prospectus.
  • Pastoral support. Who a child goes to when something's wrong. It's one of the first things anxious parents want to know.
  • The head, briefly and honestly. Parents want to know who's in charge and whether they'd trust them. A couple of minutes of a head teacher talking naturally about what they care about beats any scripted welcome.

Open day film or prospectus film: what's the difference?

An open day film is usually short, and its job is to get a family through the door. It runs on your homepage and social channels in the weeks before the open day, and it should leave people wanting to visit. Sixty to ninety seconds is plenty.

A prospectus film is longer and works more like the prospectus itself. Families watch it at home, often together, when they're comparing schools. It can carry more: the pastoral structure, the curriculum, what happens in the sixth form, how the school handles the move up from primary. Ideally both come out of the same filming days, so the cost sits on one shoot rather than two.

Parents can look up league tables in thirty seconds. What they can't look up is whether children seem happy in the corridors.

Should pupils be interviewed on camera?

Older pupils, often yes, if they want to and the right consent is in place. They're the most believable people in any school film. Don't script them. Give them a few open questions in advance, let them talk, and use what's true. A Year 10 pupil saying they were nervous in Year 7 and explaining what helped will do more for a nervous parent than any claim about pastoral care.

Younger children are usually better filmed doing things than being interviewed. It's kinder to them and it looks more natural. For staff who'll be on camera, this is how I'd prepare anyone for being filmed.

Ask a seven year old what the best thing about school is and there's a fair chance the answer's lunch. Which, honestly, fair.

How does consent work when filming children at school?

Again, this is general guidance based on common UK practice. Check everything against your own safeguarding and data protection policies, and talk to your data protection officer before you plan a shoot.

Photos and video taken for official school use, such as a prospectus or promotional material, are likely to fall under data protection law. The ICO's guidance on photos in schools says pupils, or a parent or guardian depending on the pupil's age, must be told how the images will be used, and it recommends giving pupils the chance to opt out. It also points out that consent is only one possible lawful basis, so the school should be clear from the start which one it's relying on. Twelve is given as a typical guideline for when a child can exercise their own rights, judged case by case.

Most schools already collect image permissions at admission. Those forms don't always clearly cover a promotional film that'll sit on YouTube for years, so check the wording. If it's vague, ask again for this project specifically. Parents are far more relaxed about filming when they've been told exactly what it's for.

What safeguarding steps should a school film follow?

The NSPCC's guidance on photographing and filming children is a sensible starting point for any organisation. In general practice, a school shoot should include:

  • A no-film list, checked on the day. Some children mustn't be identifiable, such as those in local authority care, adopted children, or children whose safety depends on not being found. A named member of staff should be with the crew and know who they are.
  • No names with images. Don't caption pupils with their names, and watch what's visible on exercise books, lanyards and wall displays.
  • Staff with the crew throughout. Nobody filming should be left alone with pupils.
  • Secure handling of footage. Agree where rushes are stored, who can access them and when unused footage is deleted.
  • A second look at locations. Check whether a shot gives away more than you intend, like a recognisable route home or the outside of a pupil's house.

None of this makes filming hard. It just needs planning, and a crew who'll raise it with you before you have to raise it with them.

When should a school plan its film?

Earlier than you'd think. Secondary open days mostly fall in the early autumn, and a film needs to be live a few weeks before the first one to do any work. Our films take six to ten weeks from the first conversation, and you want to film on normal teaching days rather than in the last week of term, when everything's a bit off. In practice that usually means filming in the summer term for the following autumn.

Think about the seasons too. A school in July and a school in November look like different places, and a film that's all sunshine can feel a little off to a family who visits in the rain. If you want to see what that planning looks like before you speak to anyone, our free guide Before the camera comes out walks through it. When you're ready, get in touch.

faqs.q: Do parents need to sign a new consent form for a school film?
faqs.a: Not always, but check before you assume. Most schools collect image permissions at admission, and if the wording clearly covers promotional video online for a set period, that may be enough. If it's vague or only mentions photographs, ask again for this project. As general guidance, the ICO says pupils or parents must be told how images will be used, and your data protection officer should confirm the approach.

faqs.q: How long should a school prospectus film be?
faqs.a: A prospectus film usually runs three to six minutes, long enough to cover daily life, pastoral care and the curriculum without losing a family watching at home. An open day film should be much shorter, around sixty to ninety seconds, because its job is to get people through the door. Both can come from the same filming days, which keeps the cost down.

faqs.q: Can a school keep using a film after pupils in it have left?
faqs.a: It depends on what parents and pupils were told when consent was collected, so set a clear period up front. Many schools plan for a film to run for a few years and then refresh it, which also keeps it looking current. If a family asks for their child to be removed, have a process for handling it. Your data protection policy should set out how long images are kept.

faqs.q: Should a school film include the head teacher?
faqs.a: Usually yes, briefly and unscripted. Parents want a sense of who's in charge and whether they'd trust them, and a couple of minutes of the head talking naturally about what they care about does that well. Avoid a long scripted welcome read to camera. Pupils and staff talking about daily life should carry most of the film.

items.title: Who owns the footage when you commission a film?
items.excerpt: In the UK, copyright in a commissioned film usually stays with the maker. Licences vs assignments, what a contract should cover, and why release forms matter.
items.coverAlt: A single SD card sitting in the middle of a large, empty boardroom table, with a fountain pen lying next to it and a tidy stack of contracts just out of focus at the far end
items.body:
In the UK, copyright in a commissioned film usually stays with the people who made it, unless a written agreement signed by them transfers it to you. Paying the invoice doesn't change who owns it. What you normally get is a licence, permission to use the film in agreed ways, and that licence can be very wide or surprisingly narrow. This is general guidance based on the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 and the government's own guidance. It isn't legal advice, so for a contract that matters, have a solicitor read it.

Most businesses only find this out when they want to do something new with a film. Recut it, hand it to a different agency, run it as an advert on a platform nobody mentioned at the start. That's the worst time to discover the answer.

Who owns copyright in a commissioned video in the UK?

The starting point is the Act itself. Under section 9, the authors of a film are the producer and the principal director. The producer, under section 178, is the person who makes the arrangements necessary for the film to be made. And under section 11, the author is the first owner of the copyright.

The government's guidance on ownership of copyright works spells out what that means for commissioned work: the first legal owner is the person or organisation that created it, not the commissioner, unless you agree otherwise in writing. It also warns that a commissioner may only get a limited, non-exclusive licence if nothing was agreed.

Employees are the exception. If someone on your payroll makes a film in the course of their job, section 11 makes the employer the first owner, unless there's an agreement saying otherwise. A freelancer or a production company isn't your employee, so that exception doesn't apply to them.

Paying for something you don't own sounds like a scam until you remember it's how photography and music have worked for decades.

What's the difference between a licence and an assignment?

An assignment transfers ownership. The copyright moves from the maker to you, and you can then do anything the owner could do, including licensing it to other people. Under section 90 an assignment isn't effective unless it's in writing and signed by or on behalf of the person giving it up. A line on an invoice saying "all rights to the client" is a weak place to rely on.

A licence is permission. The maker keeps the copyright and lets you use the film within whatever the licence says. It can be exclusive, meaning nobody else gets it, or non-exclusive. It can be limited by time, territory or platform, or it can cover everything forever.

For most businesses, a wide licence does everything ownership would. You can put the film on your site, your channels, your adverts and your sales decks for as long as you like. Ownership mostly matters if you plan to license the film to other people, sell it, or build a product around the footage. If one of those is on the cards, say so before the quote, because it changes the price.

A wide licence does nearly everything ownership would. A narrow one can stop you using your own film.

What should the licence in a video contract cover?

  • Platforms and media. Website, social, YouTube, paid adverts, broadcast, events. Paid advertising is the one most often left out.
  • Term. A year, five years, or indefinite.
  • Territory. UK only, or worldwide.
  • Edits. Whether you can recut it, shorten it or hand it to another editor later. Adapting a work is one of the acts copyright controls, so a licence that's silent on it leaves you guessing.
  • Third-party material. Music, stock footage and fonts usually come with their own licences, and the film's licence can't give you more than those allow.
  • The maker's own use. Whether the production company can show it in their portfolio, and whether you need anything kept confidential until launch.

Ours is simple on purpose. Every film comes with a full licence to use everything indefinitely, on every platform, and it's inside the fixed price. The music is the bit to check hardest on anyone's quote, and we've written a separate piece on music licensing for brand videos.

Does the director have any rights after you've paid?

Yes, and they're separate from copyright. The Act gives the director of a film moral rights, including, under section 77, the right to be identified when the film is shown or communicated to the public. Moral rights can be waived, but under section 87 a waiver has to be in writing and signed by the person giving them up. Plenty of commercial contracts include one. If yours doesn't, it rarely causes problems in practice, but it's worth knowing it exists.

What about the people who appear in the film?

The film's copyright says nothing about the people in it. That's what release forms are for. A release is a short written consent from each person on camera, saying they agree to appear and to the footage being used for the purposes listed. It protects you, and it's fair to them, because they know exactly what they're signing up for.

Our Barry Road film is the homeowner's own account of a full renovation. That person isn't on the builder's payroll and owes them nothing, so their signed consent is what makes the film usable in a sales conversation for years. The same goes for staff. Footage of identifiable people is personal data under UK data protection law, and people leave jobs. A release signed on the day saves an awkward conversation when someone who's since moved on is still on your homepage.

There's one more wrinkle with interviews. Spoken words can become a literary work once they're recorded, which gives the speaker an argument that they own the copyright in what they said. A well written release covers that too, by giving permission to use their words as well as their face.

What should you ask before you sign a video contract?

  • Am I getting a licence or an assignment, and what exactly does it cover?
  • Does it include paid advertising and every platform we'll use?
  • Can we recut the film ourselves, or with another company, later?
  • Are the raw files included, and if not, what would they cost?
  • Who's handling release forms for everyone on camera?
  • What licences come with the music and any stock footage?

None of this should be awkward to ask. A good production company will answer every one of those in a sentence. If you'd like to see how a film comes together from start to finish, the films page walks through it, and our free playbook, Before the camera comes out, covers the planning in more depth.

faqs.q: If we've paid for the film in full, don't we own it?
faqs.a: Not automatically. Under UK law the people who made a commissioned film are usually the first owners of its copyright, and payment alone doesn't transfer it. Ownership only moves with a written assignment signed by the owner. What you normally get instead is a licence to use the film, so the useful question is what that licence covers, not who owns it.

faqs.q: Can we hire a different editor to recut our brand film later?
faqs.a: Only if your licence allows it. Adapting a work is one of the things copyright controls, so check whether your contract lets you edit, shorten or recut the film, and whether that includes using another company. If it's silent, ask the original production company. Most will agree, but it's far easier to get it written into the contract before the shoot.

faqs.q: Does our business own videos our staff film on their phones?
faqs.a: Usually yes, if they made them in the course of their job. Section 11 of the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 makes the employer the first owner of a film made by an employee in the course of employment, unless there's an agreement saying otherwise. Footage a member of staff shoots on their own time, or a freelancer shoots for you, is a different matter.

faqs.q: Can a production company put our film in their portfolio?
faqs.a: Usually, yes. As the copyright owner they're generally free to show their own work unless your contract says otherwise. If the film covers something confidential, like a launch date or a client you can't name yet, agree an embargo or a restriction in writing before the shoot. Most companies are happy to hold back until you've gone public.

items.title: Filming craft: making the invisible process visible
items.excerpt: Craft and heritage businesses sell a process nobody sees. How to film hand work at its real speed so the price makes sense, with examples from our own films.
items.coverAlt: A workbench at dusk with a single loaded signwriting brush resting across a paint tin, a half finished gold letter on glass behind it and a stopwatch lying face down beside it
items.body:
The hard part of filming a craft or heritage business is that the value lives in the process, and the process is slow, small and mostly in someone's hands. A good craft film gets close to that work, lets it run at the speed it really happens, and has the maker explain why they do it that way. Show only the finished object and you've made a product video for something nobody can judge from a picture.

Most craft businesses have the same problem online. The work takes weeks or months, and what a customer sees is a photo of the result next to a price. The price makes no sense without the process, and the process is invisible. Film is the best tool I know for fixing that, because it can show time, touch and skill in a way a photograph can't.

Why do craft businesses need film more than most?

Because what they're selling is the part nobody sees. Online, a handmade pair of shoes and a high street pair are just two pairs of shoes. The difference is in hundreds of hours of hand work, and until somebody shows that, the price looks like a typo.

There's a bigger reason too. Heritage Crafts, the charity that tracks traditional skills in the UK, publishes a Red List of crafts at risk. Its 2025 edition covers 285 crafts, and more than half of them are rated endangered or critically endangered. If you're still doing something by hand that most of the country has stopped doing, that's a story in itself, and most people have never seen it done.

How do you film a process that takes months?

You don't try to show all of it. You pick the moments that carry the most skill, film those properly, and let the maker describe the rest.

When we filmed Carreducker, the numbers were the challenge. Deborah Carre and James Ducker make every pair by hand, from measuring the foot through to the shoe trees, and it's 210 steps and around six months from order to delivery. None of that fits in a film. So the coverage went close on the hand sewing and the bench work, at the speed it happens, and the two of them explained the rest as one conversation in front of their wall of lasts. They'd already documented all 210 steps publicly, one post at a time, years before anyone called that content. The film didn't need to repeat it. It needed to show what it's like to watch it done.

That's the general rule. A handful of processes, shot well and given room, tell a viewer more about the skill involved than a quick montage of every stage.

Why shouldn't you speed up the craft?

Because the speed is the evidence. Time lapses and fast cuts make everything look easy, and easy is the last thing you want a customer to think about something that took years to learn.

Signwriting Jack is the clearest example we've made. Hand painted signwriting has largely been replaced by vinyl, and the work is slow, precise and almost entirely in the wrist. The thing worth watching is the brush loading and a single unbroken line that either works or doesn't. Chop that into half second shots and you've thrown away the one moment where the viewer holds their breath. So we filmed close, waited, and let the shots run. Then we filmed the finished signs in place on the street, so you see where all that care ends up.

Time lapses make everything look easy, and easy is the last thing you want a customer to think.

Should the maker be in the film or just their hands?

Both, and in my view the face matters more than people expect. Hands show the skill. The person explains why anyone would choose to work this way, and that's often what a customer is really buying into.

Catherine Marche is a French goldsmith who's been designing and making bespoke jewellery in London for around twenty five years. She works only in recycled metal, holds her packaging to the same rule, remodels pieces people have stopped wearing, and teaches as well as makes. You can't photograph any of that. Jewellery films usually end up as product photography that moves, and with bespoke work the person is what the client's actually choosing. So the film is built around how she works and why, told by her at the bench and in the shop, with the bench coverage close on her hands.

A glass fronted shop full of polished metal is basically a hall of mirrors with a till. Budget extra time for the lighting.

What does a craft film need to show?

  • The hands at work. Close, steady and long enough to follow what's happening.
  • The tools and materials. Workshops are full of objects with history, and they do a lot of the storytelling for free.
  • The maker talking. Why this way, who taught them, what they won't compromise on.
  • Where the work ends up. On a shopfront, on a foot, on a hand. It closes the gap between the process and the price.
  • The sound. A brush on glass, a hammer on silver, a needle through leather. Leave it audible. Music wall to wall is the quickest way to make a craft film feel generic.

How do heritage businesses use a craft film?

The obvious place is the homepage, where it explains the price before anyone has to ask. It's also useful anywhere you'd otherwise describe the process in words: commission enquiries, trade conversations, press, exhibitions, and recruiting students if you teach. Carreducker and Catherine Marche both teach as well as make, and a film that shows the bench is a strong advert for a course.

Cut it short for social as well. Craft does unusually well in vertical video, because a satisfying process holds attention without anyone needing to explain it. Ten seconds of one clean line is often enough to stop a thumb.

It also lasts. Process doesn't date the way a campaign does. A film about how you make something will still be accurate in five years if you still make it the same way, which for a heritage business is rather the point.

How do you prepare a workshop for filming?

Mostly you don't, beyond a tidy and a conversation about what's on the bench that week. Plan the shoot around real work rather than staging it, because a piece being made for a real customer has stakes, and you can see that in the maker's concentration. Tell us what stage each job is at so we're there for the interesting bits, and expect the crew to wait rather than direct. The film runs on your timing.

If you run a craft business that people don't understand from photographs alone, have a look at our films and tell us what you make.
items.author: Earl Duncan

faqs.q: How long should a craft film be?
faqs.a: Long enough to let the work run, which for the main film usually means four to ten minutes. That gives you room to show a process at its real speed and hear the maker explain it. From the same shoot you'd also want a sixty to ninety second cut for the top of your website and several short vertical pieces, where a single clean process shot can carry a whole post.

faqs.q: Can you film in a workshop without stopping production?
faqs.a: Yes, and that's usually the better way to do it. Real work for a real customer has stakes you can't fake, so we film around what's already on the bench rather than asking for things to be staged. It helps to tell us beforehand which jobs are at which stage, so we're there for the moments worth seeing, and to expect the crew to wait rather than direct.

faqs.q: Do we have to show trade secrets in a craft film?
faqs.a: No. You decide what's on camera, and a good crew will ask before filming anything sensitive. Most of what makes a craft film compelling is the skill, the care and the time involved, none of which gives away how to copy you. If there's a technique or supplier you'd rather keep private, say so before the shoot and we'll plan the coverage around it.

faqs.q: Is a film worth it for a very small craft business?
faqs.a: It can be, as long as it's sized to the business. A full documentary is a bigger investment, starting at £15,000 + VAT for ours. If that's too much, a single shoot day covering you at the bench, the workshop and the finished pieces can still give you honest photography and short videos to use for years. Our Spotlight shoot is £795 + VAT.

items.title: How to set a video budget, then share the number
items.excerpt: How to set a video budget from what the film needs to achieve, what it should cover, and why telling your production company the number gets a better film.
items.coverAlt: A tape measure stretched across a production desk next to a clapperboard and a calculator, as if someone is measuring the film itself
items.body:
Set a video budget by working back from what the film needs to achieve and what that result is worth to your business, then sense-check it against what that kind of film costs on the market. Once you have a number, tell your production company. A real figure gets you a proposal built around it, instead of a guess that's either too big to sign or too small to be any good.

I know telling a supplier your budget feels like giving away your hand. I'd still argue it's the single most useful thing you can do at the start, and I'll explain why below. First, the number itself.

Why is a video budget so hard to set?

Most people don't buy video often, so there's nothing to compare against. Quotes for what sounds like the same brief can run from a couple of thousand pounds to tens of thousands, and both ends can be fair. Faced with that, people tend to do one of two things. They pick a number out of the air, or they refuse to give one and wait to see what comes back. Both make the whole process slower and the proposals harder to compare.

How do you work out what a film is worth to you?

Start with the goal. What is one more of the thing you want actually worth? One extra client, one good hire, one sold-out event, one partner signed. Say a typical client is worth £10,000 to you over the relationship. If a film helps your team win two or three more a year, it's easy to see what you can sensibly spend.

Then think about how long it'll work for. A documentary-style film about your founder or your craft can still be doing its job three years from now. A reel built on this month's trend is finished in a fortnight. Spread the cost across the years you'll use it and the number often looks more reasonable than it did at first.

Last, look at what you already spend chasing the same result. Exhibition stands, recruiter fees, ad spend, sales hours lost explaining the same things on every call. If a film takes some of that load, it's really drawing on money you already spend.

What does a video budget need to cover?

More than the shoot day. When you set your number, make sure it covers:

  • Research and pre-production. Working out the story, who's in it and where. This is what decides whether the film is any good.
  • Shoot days and crew. The biggest single cost, because most other costs scale with it.
  • Locations and travel. Free on your own premises, which is one reason documentary can be good value.
  • Edit, grade and sound mix. Where most of the hours actually go.
  • Music licence. Check what it covers and for how long.
  • Cut-downs and formats. Short versions, verticals and subtitled versions.
  • Distribution. If the film is going to run as an ad, the media money is separate and matters as much as the production money.

Our free film budget calculator walks through those lines if you want to rough out a number before you speak to anyone. For what each budget level typically buys in the UK, I've written a full breakdown in how much a brand film costs.

Why should you tell your production company the number?

Because without it, they have to guess, and guessing helps nobody. Some will design the film they'd love to make and price it. Others will quote low to win the job and claw it back later in extras. You end up comparing three proposals that aren't for the same thing, which means you can't really compare them at all.

With a number, the question changes to "what's the best film we can make for this?" That's a far better question, and a decent production company will make trade-offs in your favour to answer it. One shoot day instead of two, with more time in the edit. Your own premises instead of a hired location. No drone, because it adds nothing to this story. The budget becomes a design constraint, and constraints usually make the creative sharper.

The budget becomes a design constraint, and constraints usually make the creative sharper.

Our Car Planet customer story is a good example of decisions shaped by limits. Everything was captured in a single visit, so the cost sat on one day rather than three. The client didn't want the site on display, so we framed tight on the work and filled the edit with b-roll from previous installs and their own image bank, cut so the joins don't show.

Won't they just spend all of it?

It's a fair worry, and I'd rather answer it straight. A good company will tell you when the job needs less than you've said, because a client who feels stretched doesn't come back. They'll also tell you when it needs more, and why, before anything's booked. That's the trade I want with anyone I work with. Fair to you, clear for us.

Keeping your budget secret to get a better price is a bit like hiding your shoe size to get better shoes.

To protect yourself, ask for one fixed figure agreed in full before anything's booked, with the deliverables written down. Then you're comparing what's included, not just the total.

What if you genuinely don't know your number?

Give a range and a ceiling. "Somewhere between £8,000 and £15,000, and fifteen is a hard stop" is plenty to work with. If that still feels impossible, tell them what you've spent on comparable marketing, like a trade show or a quarter of ads. Anything is better than nothing, because it stops either side wasting weeks on something that was never going to happen.

And if your number is small, say so anyway. If it's £3,000, a good company will either shape something sensible around it or point you to someone better suited. Both save you time.

How do you stop a video budget creeping?

Most overruns come from decisions made late. Agree the deliverables, the number of revision rounds and the licence up front. Decide who signs the film off before the shoot, because a new voice at the final cut is the most expensive kind of feedback there is. Give your notes at rough cut, while changes are cheap, rather than after the picture is locked. And resist adding a second location or an extra interviewee halfway through. If it genuinely matters, ask for it to be quoted as a change before anyone does the work.

If you've got a number in mind and a business with a story in it, tell us both. Our films start at £15,000 + VAT, and if that's not the right spend for what you need, I'll tell you what is.

faqs.q: What percentage of a marketing budget should go on video?
faqs.a: There's no fixed rule, and anyone giving you one is guessing about your business. Work from the job instead. If video is doing heavy lifting in sales, hiring or a launch, it deserves a bigger share than if it's an occasional social post. In Wyzowl's 2026 survey the largest group of marketers, 46%, put a third of their budget or less into video, which is a reasonable sense check.

faqs.q: Should the video budget include ad spend?
faqs.a: Keep them as two separate lines. Production pays for the film itself, and ad spend pays for people to see it. If the film's main job is paid advertising, the media budget can be as important as the production budget, so plan both at the start. A great film with nothing behind it reaches very few people, and a big ad budget behind a weak film wastes money faster.

faqs.q: Is it cheaper to film several videos in one day?
faqs.a: Usually, yes. The shoot day carries most of the cost, so capturing a main film, cut-downs, verticals and photography on the same visit spreads it across far more content. The catch is planning. Each piece needs its own shots, framing and questions, so tell your production company everything you want before the shoot rather than asking for extras from footage that was never captured for them.

faqs.q: How many quotes should you get for a video?
faqs.a: Two or three is plenty, as long as each company gets the same brief and the same budget. That's what makes them comparable. Then compare what's included rather than the total: research, shoot days, crew, edit time, grade and mix, music licence, cut-downs and usage rights. The cheapest quote often leaves out the parts that decide whether the film is any good.

items.title: Music licensing for brand videos, explained
items.excerpt: Why businesses get copyright claims on their videos, library vs commercial music, and what a music licence really covers: term, territory and platform.
items.coverAlt: A pair of studio headphones hung on a hook beside a fat ring binder labelled only by a coloured spine, on a cluttered edit desk lit by a single lamp, the binder bristling with sticky notes
items.body:
Businesses get copyright claims on their videos because a piece of music was used without a licence that covers that use, that platform or that length of time. Usually nobody meant any harm. Someone picked a track they liked, a library licence ran out, or a social edit got posted somewhere the licence never reached. What follows is general guidance from how music licensing works in production. It isn't legal advice, so if there's real money or a live dispute involved, talk to a solicitor or the rights holder directly.

Music is the part of a film people think about last and argue about most. It's also the part most likely to come back a year later, when the film's doing well and somebody's software finally notices it.

Why do businesses get copyright claims on their videos?

Mostly because of automated matching. On YouTube, every upload is scanned by Content ID, which compares it against audio and video that rights holders have registered. When it finds a match, the owner chooses what happens: block the video, run ads on it and take the money, or just track the viewing figures. Those choices can differ from country to country, so a film can play fine in the UK and be blocked somewhere else.

Letters and emails are the other route. Rights holders, and firms that work on their behalf, look for their music on business websites and social channels and write asking for a licence fee. That's a lot less pleasant than a YouTube notification, because it usually comes with a number attached.

The causes are boringly familiar:

  • A commercial track on a business post. The trending sound everyone's using is licensed for personal accounts, not for your company.
  • The wrong library for the account. TikTok's own commercial music terms say its Commercial Sounds are the only sounds available for commercial use, and only within TikTok. Meta has its own Sound Collection too, so check which library your account is drawing from.
  • A licence that didn't travel. The edit was made for one platform with that platform's music, then uploaded to YouTube or LinkedIn with the track still on it.
  • A licence in somebody else's name. A freelancer's or an old agency's subscription covered the original upload, and nobody checked whether it covered you.
  • A subscription that stopped. Some libraries keep you covered for anything published while you were paying. Some don't. The terms decide, so read them.

A track that “just felt right” in the edit feels a lot less right on an invoice from a music publisher.

What's the difference between library music and commercial music?

Every recorded track carries two copyrights. One is in the song itself, the melody and lyrics written by the composer. The other is in the recording, the actual performance the label paid to make. In the UK, PPL and PRS for Music look after those two sides for broadcast and public performance, which is a handy way to see that they're separate things.

To put a commercial track in a brand film, you need permission for both. A sync licence from the publisher for the song, and a master licence from the label for the recording. That takes time, it costs real money for anything people would recognise, and either side can simply say no. Big brands do it because a famous song does a specific job for them. For most businesses it's the wrong fight.

Library music, sometimes called production music, is written to be used in films and adverts. The library owns or controls both sides, so one licence covers the lot. You pay per project or by subscription, and the terms are written down before you start. The quality at the good end is excellent. The quality at the cheap end sounds like a hold queue.

One thing that catches people out. TheMusicLicence from PPL PRS lets a business play music in its premises, to staff and customers. It's for the radio in the shop. Putting a track inside a film is a different use, and that licence doesn't cover it.

Royalty free means you don't pay per play. It doesn't mean nobody owns it.

What does a music licence actually cover?

Every music licence draws a box around what you're allowed to do. The four edges of that box are the things to read:

  • Term. How long you can use it. Perpetual, a year, or only while a subscription is live.
  • Territory. Where it can be shown. Worldwide is common for online use, but not universal, and commercial tracks are often cleared country by country.
  • Platform and media. Website and social only, or also broadcast, cinema, events and trade shows. A licence that covers organic social posts may not cover paid adverts on the same platforms.
  • The project. One film, or the film plus its cut-downs. If you're getting a sixty second version and a run of vertical edits, check the licence covers every one of them.

There are smaller questions inside those, like whether the track can be cut, looped or faded, and whose name the licence is in. That last one matters more than it sounds. If the licence belongs to the production company, ask what happens when you use the film on your own channels for years after the job is done.

Is royalty free music actually free to use?

No. Royalty free means you pay once, or pay a subscription, instead of paying every time the film is played. You still need a licence, and the licence still has edges.

It also doesn't mean you'll never see a claim. Some libraries register their tracks with Content ID, so a properly licensed film can still get flagged. That's usually sorted by sending the library your licence details so they can clear your channel, or by disputing the claim with the licence attached. Annoying, fixable, and a good reason to keep the paperwork somewhere you can find it.

Can you use AI generated music in a brand film?

You can, with two checks. First, the tool's terms. They vary on whether you can use the output commercially and what you actually own, so read them before the track goes anywhere near a client film. Second, disclosure. YouTube's rules on altered or synthetic content ask creators to disclose generated music when it's the main focus of the video. For a bed under an interview that's less of an issue, but it's worth knowing the rule is there.

Do you always need music in a brand video?

Honestly, no. Some of the best moments in a film are the sound of the work. When we cut the vertical edits for Super Efficient, the jetter and the water were left alone rather than buried under a track, because the sound is half of why people watch a drain clear.

That's the longform film from the same day. Music has a job in it, but it never fights the people or the work. In an interview-led film the voice matters most, and music sits under it.

What should you ask about the music before you sign off a film?

  • Is it library music or a commercial track, and who licensed it?
  • Whose name is on the licence, and can I have a copy?
  • Does it cover paid adverts as well as organic posts?
  • Does it cover every cut-down and every platform we'll use?
  • How long does it last, and what happens if a subscription stops?
  • Is the track registered with Content ID, and how do we clear a claim if one comes up?

On our films, the licence covers everything indefinitely on every platform, so the music has to be chosen to fit that from the start. We go into how licensing sits inside a film budget in how much a brand film costs in the UK, and if you've got a film coming up and want a second pair of eyes on the music, get in touch.
